content: Fingerspelling, also referred to as dactylology, is the representation of the letters of a writing system, and sometimes numerical systems, using only the hands. Various manual alphabets, also known as finger alphabets or hand alphabets, have been developed and used historically and in modern times, particularly in the context of deaf education. These alphabets have subsequently been incorporated as distinct components of numerous sign languages worldwide. Fingerspelling can be understood either visually or tactually. The simplest visual form involves tracing the shapes of letters in the air, while the tactile form involves tracing letters onto the palm. However, most manual alphabets employ unique hand signs to represent individual letters. These signs are distinguished by specific handshapes, palm orientations, and sometimes by movement, location, or accompanying mouth patterns. The handshapes are often stylized representations of the written letter forms but may also be arbitrary signs or a combination of iconic and arbitrary elements. Manual alphabets exist for a variety of scripts, including Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Devanagari, Bengali, Arabic, Hebrew, Thai, Hangul, Kanji, Kana, and Ge'ez. Additionally, related manual systems have been developed to phonetically represent sounds rather than the written forms of spoken languages. These systems, sometimes referred to as Mouth Hand Systems (MHS), include Cued Speech and a unique MHS created in Denmark in 1903 by Georg Forchhammer. Fingerspelling in Sign Languages Fingerspelling has been introduced into certain sign languages by educators, both deaf and hearing. It possesses structural properties that differ from the visually motivated and multi-layered signs typical of native deaf sign languages. In many cases, fingerspelling acts as a bridge between the sign language and the surrounding spoken language. It is used for various purposes, such as representing words without a sign equivalent, emphasizing or clarifying concepts, or teaching and learning sign language. In American Sign Language (ASL), fingerspelling is more commonly used in casual conversation than in formal or narrative signing. Different sign language communities use fingerspelling to varying extents. For example, 7% of casual signing in ASL and 10% in Auslan (Australian Sign Language) involves fingerspelling. Older signers tend to use fingerspelling more frequently, suggesting its usage has declined over time. In New Zealand Sign Language (NZSL), only 5% of the corpus involves fingerspelling, which became part of the language only in the 1980s. Before that, letters were traced in the air for spelling or initialization. Fingerspelling is less commonly used in the sign languages of Eastern Europe, except in schools, and Italian Sign Language employs it sparingly, mainly for foreign words. Some sign languages, such as Kata Kolok and Ban Khor Sign Language, do not use fingerspelling at all. The speed and clarity of fingerspelling vary across signing communities. For instance, in Italian Sign Language, fingerspelled words are produced slowly and clearly, while in British Sign Language (BSL), fingerspelling is often rapid, making individual letters difficult to distinguish. In such cases, the overall hand movement conveys the word. In BSL, most letters are produced with two hands, but when one hand is occupied, the dominant hand may fingerspell onto an imaginary subordinate hand, with the word recognized through movement. Fluent signers typically maintain eye contact and look at the signer’s face rather than their hands when reading fingerspelling, as is customary in sign language communication. In contrast, learners often need to look directly at the signer’s hand and may require the signer to slow down. Mastery of fingerspelling, both expressively and receptively, often takes years of practice. History Some scholars have suggested that the body and hands were used to represent alphabets in ancient Greek, Roman, Egyptian, and Assyrian cultures. Finger calculus systems, capable of representing numbers up to 10,000, were widespread and remain in use in parts of the Middle East. The substitution of letters for numbers and vice versa, known as gematria, was also common and may have been combined with finger calculus to create a finger calculus alphabet. The earliest known manual alphabet was described by the Benedictine monk Bede in 8th-century Northumbria. This alphabet substituted letters for numbers and was likely not used by deaf individuals for communication, despite Bede losing his hearing later in life. Historian Lois Bragg concluded that these alphabets were likely only a bookish game. Some writers, beginning with R.A.S. Macalister in 1938, speculated that the 5th-century Irish Ogham script, with its quinary alphabet system, was derived from an earlier finger alphabet predating Bede. European monks, at least since Bede’s time, used forms of manual communication, including alphabetic gestures, for various purposes: silent communication within monasteries, administering to the ill, mnemonic devices, and possibly as ciphers for discreet or secret communication. Clear antecedents of many modern manual alphabets can be traced to the 16th century in books published by friars in Spain and Italy. During this period, monks like the Benedictine Fray Pedro Ponce de León began tutoring deaf children of wealthy patrons, using manual alphabets to teach literacy, which was often a legal requirement for inheritance. The first book on deaf education, published in 1620 in Madrid, detailed the use of a manual alphabet to teach deaf students to read and speak. In Britain, manual alphabets were used for secret communication, public speaking, and communication by deaf individuals. In 1648, John Bulwer described a deaf man proficient in a manual alphabet devised on the joints of his fingers, which his wife could understand even in the dark through tactile signing. In 1680, George Dalgarno published Didascalocophus, presenting his method of deaf education, including an arthrological alphabet where letters were indicated by pointing to different joints of the left hand. Arthrological systems had been used by hearing people for some time and may trace back to early Ogham manual alphabets. The vowels of this alphabet survive in contemporary alphabets used in BSL, Auslan, and NZSL. The earliest printed depictions of consonants from the modern two-handed alphabet appeared in 1698 in Digiti Lingua, a pamphlet by an anonymous author who suggested the manual alphabet could be used by mutes for silence, secrecy, or entertainment. By 1720, the British manual alphabet had taken its present form, and its descendants have been used by deaf communities in former British colonies and other regions. Latin Alphabet Two families of manual alphabets are used to represent the Latin alphabet in the modern world. The more common one-handed alphabet can be traced back to alphabetic signs used in Europe from at least the early 15th century. This alphabet, first fully described by Spanish monks, was adopted by the Abbé de l'Épée’s deaf school in Paris in the 18th century and spread globally in the 19th and 20th centuries through educators trained there. Variations have since emerged due to phonetic changes, adaptations for local written forms, and avoidance of handshapes considered obscene in some cultures. Modern descendants include the American manual alphabet and the International manual alphabet. Several two-handed manual alphabets are also used by deaf communities worldwide. In some regions, such as the former Yugoslavia and Turkish Sign Language, vowels are represented by iconic signs, while in the BANZSL group of languages, they are represented by pointing to the fingertips. Other Alphabets Manual alphabets based on the Arabic alphabet, the Ethiopian syllabary, and the Korean Hangul syllabary-alphabet use handshapes that are more or less iconic representations of the characters in their respective writing systems. Some manual representations of non-Roman scripts, such as Chinese, Japanese, Indian Nagari, Hebrew, Greek, Thai, and Russian alphabets, are partially based on the one-handed Roman alphabet.
